newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pressure mounts on Zeroual over Algerian conflict.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Zeroual over Algerian conflict.

text.p: Political pressure is growing on Algerian President Liamine Zeroual to try to end an increasingly bloody conflict, which he himself says is claiming new victims every day.
Political analysts said that after two particularly violent weeks, which left about 250 bodies for burial, Zeroual's government is under internal and external pressure to act.
In the bomb-blasted streets of Algiers, where shopowners laid concrete blocks as obstacles against Moslem fundamentalist car bombs, there is anger mixed with resignation.
"They don't seem to be doing anything except stopping those people who call for peace," said one middle-aged man at a wreath-laying ceremony in Belcourt on Sunday to victims of a bomb last week.

In the old parliament building on Algiers corniche, even government-appointed members of the unelected quasi-parliament are speaking out against the authorities' plans to tighten political laws ahead of a general election.
"If we endorse this law as it is, we will sign our political death sentence," said a spokesman for a dozen small parties within the near 200-member National Transitional Council (CNT).

The law sets the basis for political parties allowed to contest a general election promised before July this year. It bans parties based on religion or language, and demands widespread representation with minimum support in at least 25 provinces of the country's 48.

Opposition politicians too this weekend denounced lack of action or any announcement in the president's nationwide Friday night address of measures to end bloodshed. Zeroual vowed the state would eradicate "terrorism" but announced no new steps to do so.
The latest reported killing took place on Sunday. Three men shot dead an activist with the opposition Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD). The dead man was father of five children.
Pressure, or at least expressions of concern, is increasing also overseas.

In Paris, old colonial master of Algeria, Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin called for action on the violence in Algeria in which about 60,000 have died since the authorities early in 1992 scrapped an election dominated by Islamists.

Jospin, in remarks published on Monday, said: "The Algerian government will overcome terrorism, modernise the country and return some hope to the population only if it accepts some change and particularly dialogue with democratic forces."
He urged France to consult its European partners on a joint initiative, saying no one dared discuss Algeria as long as Paris did not move.

But in Copenhagen, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said: "Algeria is an independent country and for the moment we think it is the responsibility of the Algerian people, Algerian leaders, to find solutions to their own problems."
France, the main backer of Algeria's authorities, is known to be nervous of public involvement in its former territory from which it was ousted in 1962 after a bloody eight-year war.
Bombs have hit Paris and Algerian rebels have warned French leaders against supporting Algiers.
France is particularly concerned about the possibility of a wave of Algerians fleeing across the Mediterranean to escape bloodshed to add to its North African population of more than one million.
